prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands 4 columns to the right of the chosen anchor, wrapping around: a brick chosen at column x lands at column (x + 4) mod 8, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
No trials have been run in this search yet. In generation 0, all 84 trials across 7 worlds scored 0, both on dev and in training, so there is still no measure of seed noise and no ranking of ideas. Training success was also 0, so the agent fails to learn at all; this is not a generalisation problem. Recipe settings, attention and layout-free heads have already been tested, and repeating them would add little. These areas are still untested: lr above 2e-3, n_envs above 256, gae_lambda below 0.9, normalisation layers, PPO-style orthogonal initialisation with small policy outputs, global context fed back into per-cell features, and footprint heads that see every cell under the brick separately rather than only pooled summaries. This round places three different bets, each aimed at the first nonzero signal: an aggressive large-batch, high-lr recipe; a normalised network whose heads see each footprint cell separately; and a pure change to the initialisation.

### Round 2
Every trial so far, in generation 0 and in round 1, scored exactly 0 on dev and 0 on training success. The round 1 trials were a large-batch recipe with high lr, normalised per-cell footprint heads, and PPO orthogonal init. Seed noise still cannot be measured. Training itself fails, so the bottleneck is learning at all, not generalisation. A likely trap: random placements mostly add extra cells and earn negative reward, so the agent learns an early DONE. Only an exact build earns the +1 bonus. Untried directions are worth more than refining a baseline that scores 0. This round tests three of them: (1) many more cheap updates, using a tiny network with 1 epoch and lr 3e-3, which was never tried above 2e-3; (2) long-horizon credit, with gamma 0.995 and lambda 0.97, so the terminal bonus propagates; (3) a structured head that learns each column's height distribution and which layers are safe to fill, then scores each placement by its expected landing layer.

### Round 3
All 6 trials scored 0.000 dev success and 0 training success on both seeds, as did all 84 trials in generation 0. Since every score is 0, seed noise is unknown and no idea can be ranked. These changes all failed: large batches with lr 3e-3 and gamma 0.9, a normed net with footprint-concatenation heads, orthogonal init, a tiny net with 1 epoch, gamma 0.995, and a structured landing-layer head. Two causes have not been tested. The first is too few gradient steps per sample: earlier runs made at most about 1.6k optimiser steps. The second is that this world may differ from the description, for example in action layout or DONE index. If so, conv heads would point at the wrong actions. This round tests three things: many optimiser steps per sample, a layout-free residual over every action logit, and strong exploration.

### Round 4
Of 9 trials, only r3c2 scored above zero: one seed built 2 of 512 dev designs and training success was 0.002. That could be luck, but it is the only signal so far. Recipe changes failed across the board: large batches, 1 epoch with many optimiser steps, long horizons, strong entropy and orthogonal init all scored 0. A structured landing-layer head and per-cell footprint heads also scored 0. What r3c2 added was a zero-initialised dense residual covering every action logit, DONE included. It gives each action its own learned bias, adds non-local capacity, and can correct a possible mismatch between action indices and grid cells in a world that "may not behave as described". This is the last round, and anything scoring above 0.002 wins. So all three candidates build on r3c2's dense path: a wider dense input, more samples through 1 PPO epoch, and a linear shortcut from the raw observation to every logit.

## Trial it ended with
name: Conv head plus layout-free residual
hypothesis: This world may not match its description, for example in action-index layout or DONE position. If so, conv heads would map logits to the wrong actions. This adds a zero-initialised dense Linear over flattened conv features to all n_actions logits (DONE included). It can fix any index mismatch, and the conv prior is kept where the layout is right. Recipe: orthogonal init, 2 epochs, lr 2e-3. Refuted if both seeds stay at 0.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

reply.evidence: Round 3 suggests the world "may differ from the description, for example in action layout or DONE index", so that "conv heads would point at the wrong actions". Round 4 and the final trial repeat the idea of a "mismatch between action indices and grid cells". That is the right kind of change: actions land somewhere other than the chosen cell. But it stays a hedged guess, and the text never says placements shift 4 columns to the right with wraparound.
